claims.source: Notably, the FER protein has been shown to be aberrantly upregulated and activated in different types of carcinoma (Yang et al., 2009; Zoubeidi et al., 2009; Albeck and Brugge, 2011; Ren et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Yang et al., 2009; Zoubeidi et al., 2009; Albeck and Brugge, 2011; Ren et al., 2012.

claims.claim: High activity of FER protein kinase has been observed in 22% of ovarian cancer tumor samples via a global phosphoproteomic approach.
claims.source: Specifically, high activity of FER protein kinase has been observed in 22% of ovarian cancer tumor samples via a global phosphoproteomic approach (Ren et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ren et al., 2012.

claims.claim: STAT3, cortactin, MET, and CRMP2 have been verified as FER substrates.
claims.source: Meanwhile, STAT3, cortactin, MET, and CRMP2, the functions of which are intensively involved in tumor cell motility and chemo-resistance, have been verified as FER substrates (Orlovsky et al., 2002; Fan et al., 2004; Zheng et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Orlovsky et al., 2002; Fan et al., 2004; Zheng et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: FER expression has been associated with proliferation of tumor cells.
claims.source: In addition to motility, FER expression has also been associated with proliferation of tumor cells (Zoubeidi et al., 2009; Allard et al., 2000; Lennartsson et al., 2013; Oneyama et al., 2016; Ivanova et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Zoubeidi et al., 2009; Allard et al., 2000; Lennartsson et al., 2013; Oneyama et al., 2016; Ivanova et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Significant numbers of proteins could be modified by tyrosine phosphorylation in cells expressing FER-WT compared to FER-K591R.
claims.source: We observed that significant numbers of proteins could be modified by tyrosine phosphorylation in cells expressing FER-WT compared to FER-K591R (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: 2298 candidate substrates with scores above 100 were obtained from in-gel tryptic digestion mass spectrometry analysis.
claims.source: We obtained 2298 candidate substrates with scores above 100 (Figure 1B and Supplementary files 1-6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data referenced in Figure 1B and supplementary files.

claims.claim: 153 candidate proteins were identified from on-bead tryptic digestion followed by mass spectrometry.
claims.source: With this procedure we identified 153 candidate proteins (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data referenced in Figure 1B and supplementary file 7.

claims.claim: 99 overlapped hits were obtained by combining results from two mass spectrometry experiments.
claims.source: Combining results from the two experiments, we obtained 99 overlapped hits for further examination (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: FER was identified as its own substrate since the Tyr402 residue of the kinase is known to be auto-phosphorylated.
claims.source: Notably, we identified FER as its own substrate since the Tyr402 residue of the kinase is known to be auto-phosphorylated (Fan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fan et al., 2016.

claims.claim: IGF1R was identified as a candidate FER substrate.
claims.source: We also identified IGF1R, a key tyrosine kinase receptor in regulating cancer cell survival, proliferation, and motility (Stanicka et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and a citation to Stanicka et al., 2018 for IGF1R function.

claims.claim: IRS4 binds to FER.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 2A–B, IRS4 binds to FER and this association was not affected when FER-WT was replaced with its kinase-dead mutant FER-K591R.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claims.claim: The association between IRS4 and FER was not affected when FER-WT was replaced with its kinase-dead mutant FER-K591R.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 2A–B, IRS4 binds to FER and this association was not affected when FER-WT was replaced with its kinase-dead mutant FER-K591R.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claims.claim: The binding of GRB2 to IRS4 was FER kinase activity-dependent.
claims.source: Interestingly, the binding of GRB2 to IRS4 was FER kinase activity-dependent (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The shortest truncation of IRS4 (1–400) maintained a similar binding affinity with FER.
claims.source: Surprisingly, the shortest truncation of IRS4 (1–400) maintained a similar binding affinity with FER, indicating the N-terminal region of IRS4 is crucial for the interaction (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The N-terminal region of IRS4 is crucial for the interaction with FER.
claims.source: Surprisingly, the shortest truncation of IRS4 (1–400) maintained a similar binding affinity with FER, indicating the N-terminal region of IRS4 is crucial for the interaction (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the binding data of truncation mutants shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The 335–400 and 401–1257 mutants of IRS4 demonstrated no binding affinity with FER.
claims.source: Whereas the 335–400 and 401–1257 mutants demonstrated no binding affinity with FER, the 200–400 mutant maintained weak but substantial interaction with FER (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The 200–400 mutant of IRS4 maintained weak but substantial interaction with FER.
claims.source: Whereas the 335–400 and 401–1257 mutants demonstrated no binding affinity with FER, the 200–400 mutant maintained weak but substantial interaction with FER (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The N-terminal 1–334aa of IRS4 showed strongest binding among all truncated constructs tested.
claims.source: The N-terminal mutant 1–334 showed strongest binding among all these truncated constructs (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Both PH and PTB domains of IRS4 are involved in binding with FER.
claims.source: However, all three mutants showed as strong binding affinity with FER as WT IRS4, suggesting both PH and PTB domains were involved (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Deletion of PH or PTB domain has minimal effect on binding affinity of IRS4 with FER.
claims.source: Interestingly, deletion of PH or PTB domain has minimal effect on binding affinity with FER (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), suggesting disrupt either of these domains is not sufficient to collapse the protein complex.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The C-terminal region (447–822aa, SH2+ kinase domains) of FER showed robust interaction with IRS4.
claims.source: The C-terminal region (447–822aa, SH2+ kinase domains) of FER, rather than its N-terminal region (1–446aa, F-BAR+ FX domains), showed robust interaction with IRS4 (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The N-terminal region (1–446aa, F-BAR+ FX domains) of FER did not show interaction with IRS4.
claims.source: The C-terminal region (447–822aa, SH2+ kinase domains) of FER, rather than its N-terminal region (1–446aa, F-BAR+ FX domains), showed robust interaction with IRS4 (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: FER kinase domain, but not SH2 domain, was involved in interaction with IRS4.
claims.source: Notably, FER kinase domain, but not SH2 domain, was involved in interaction with IRS4 (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: FER kinase domain showed strong interaction with either PH domain (1–200aa) or PTB domain (200–400aa) of IRS4.
claims.source: Furthermore, FER kinase domain, but not SH2 domain, showed strong interaction with either PH domain (1–200aa) or PTB domain (200–400aa) of IRS4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-D.

claims.claim: Among seven non-receptor tyrosine kinases tested, FER illustrated highest capability for tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3A, among all these kinases, FER illustrated highest capability for tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: IRS4 is a bona fide FER substrate.
claims.source: This result demonstrates that IRS4 is a bona fide FER substrate.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The tyrosine phosphorylation level of IRS4 was increased in an FER kinase dosage-dependent manner.
claims.source: The tyrosine phosphorylation level of IRS4 was increased in an FER kinase dosage-dependent manner (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Tyrosine residues between 700 and 1093 amino acids of IRS4 were potential substrate(s) for FER kinase.
claims.source: We concluded tyrosine residues between 700 and 1093 amino acids of IRS4 were potential substrate(s) for FER kinase, since: (1) the 1–1093 mutant of IRS4 showed equivalent phosphorylation level to full-length IRS4 upon FER phosphorylation; (2) compared to the 1–699 mutant, 1–800 mutant of IRS4 showed weak but significant amount of phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from phosphorylation data of IRS4 truncation mutants shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Three tyrosine sites, Y656, Y828, and Y921, were repeatedly detected as phosphorylated in both mass spectrometry datasets.
claims.source: By performing mass spectrometry analysis in duplicate, we observed three tyrosine sites, namely Y656, Y828, and Y921, whose phosphorylation were repeatedly detected in both datasets (Figure 3D and Supplementary files 8-9).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D and supplementary files 8-9.

claims.claim: Y847 was detected as phosphorylated once in mass spectrometry analysis.
claims.source: Y847 was also detected once (Figure 3D and Supplementary file 8).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D and supplementary file 8.

claims.claim: A tyrosine to phenylalanine substitution at residue 779 remarkably decreased the phosphorylation level of IRS4 in the presence of FER.
claims.source: Excluding the Y828, Y847, and Y921 mutants, a tyrosine to phenylalanine substitution at residue 779 remarkably decreased the phosphorylation level of IRS4 in the presence of FER (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The tyrosine phosphorylation level of 5YF mutant by FER was profoundly diminished compared to each single mutant.
claims.source: The tyrosine phosphorylation level of 5YF mutant by FER was profoundly diminished compared to each single mutant (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: There are five major tyrosine residues within IRS4 that are subjected to FER-mediated phosphorylation.
claims.source: These results highly suggest that there are five major tyrosine residues within IRS4 that are subjected to FER-mediated phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from mass spectrometry and mutagenesis data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Two ovarian carcinoma-derived cell lines, OVCAR-5 and OVCAR-3, showed evident upregulation of IRS4 protein expression compared to normal HOSE control cells.
claims.source: Compared to normal HOSE control cells, two ovarian carcinoma-derived cell lines, OVCAR-5 and OVCAR-3, showed evident upregulation of IRS4 protein expression (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The expression of IRS4 significantly elevated the proliferation capacity of HEY and OVCAR-8 cells.
claims.source: Notably, Cell Titer-Glo (CTG) luminescent cell viability assay demonstrated that the expression of IRS4 significantly elevated the proliferation capacity of these cells (Figure 4C and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4C and E.

claims.claim: Loss of IRS4 has minimal effect on OVCAR-5 cell survival.
claims.source: Results from Annexin V-FITC and propidium iodide (PI) double staining assay indicated that loss of IRS4 has minimal effect on OVCAR-5 cell survival (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Annexin V-FITC and PI staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Loss of IRS4 significantly decreased the proportion of cells within S phase.
claims.source: Further cell cycle analysis in both WT and IRS4 KO cell lines with PI staining indicated that loss of IRS4 significantly decreased the proportion of cells within S phase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C.

claims.claim: The KO of IRS4 notably delayed the proliferation capacity of OVCAR-5 cells.
claims.source: Consistently, CTG assay demonstrated that the KO of IRS4 notably delayed the proliferation capacity of OVCAR-5 cells (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Ectopic re-expression of IRS4, rather than an empty vector, restored the potential of cell proliferation in IRS4-KO ovarian cancer cells.
claims.source: Ectopic re-expression of IRS4, rather than an empty vector, restored the potential of cell proliferation in IRS4-KO ovarian cancer cells (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Loss of IRS4 in OVCAR-3 cells led to growth retardation.
claims.source: Consistent with KO studies in OVCAR-5 cells, loss of IRS4 in OVCAR-3 cells also led to growth retardation (Figure 4J), highlighting the key role of IRS4 in maintaining ovarian tumor cell growth.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4J.

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of IRS4 significantly elevated the level of phospho-AKT in HEY and OVCAR-8 cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, ectopic expression of IRS4 significantly elevated the level of phospho-AKT in HEY and OVCAR-8 cells (Figure 4B and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4B and D.

claims.claim: A dramatic decrease of phospho-AKT was observed in both OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells and OVCAR-3 IRS4-KD cells.
claims.source: Consistently, we also observed a dramatic decrease of phospho-AKT in both OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells (Figure 4F) and OVCAR-3 IRS4-KD cells (Figure 4I), indicating a tight correlation between PI3K-AKT pathway and ovarian cancer cell proliferation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4F and 4I.

claims.claim: The inhibition of the PI3K-AKT pathway in OVCAR-5 cells decreased the phosphorylation level of AKT and cell growth in a concentration-dependent manner.
claims.source: To confirm this, we treated OVCAR-5 WT cells with PI3K inhibitor LY294002 (Figure 4K–L) and demonstrated that the inhibition of the PI3K-AKT pathway in OVCAR-5 cells indeed decreased the phosphorylation level of AKT and cell growth in a concentration-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting and cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4K-L.

claims.claim: 16 out of 30 compounds that showed proliferation inhibition greater than 75% targeted the PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling pathway.
claims.source: Thirty out of 198 compounds showed proliferation inhibition greater than 75% (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A). Among these, 16 compounds targeted the PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling pathway (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by compound library screening data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B.

claims.claim: Evident elevation in phospho-ERK level was observed in OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, whereas there was a dramatic decrease of phospho-AKT signal upon IRS4 deletion, we also observed evident elevation in phospho-ERK level in OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells (Figure 4F), indicating a potential compensatory effect of ERK signaling pathway which may contribute to the survival and proliferative capacities of OVCAR-5 cancer cells after IRS4 deletion.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The inhibition of both PI3K-AKT pathway and ERK pathway in OVCAR-5 cells almost blocked cell growth completely.
claims.source: The inhibition of both PI3K-AKT pathway and ERK pathway in OVCAR-5 cells almost blocked cell growth completely (Figure 4M).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 4M.

claims.claim: PIK3R2 preferred to bind with WT rather than the Y779F mutant of IRS4.
claims.source: Notably, we observed that PIK3R2 (the regulatory subunit of PI3K) preferred to bind with WT rather than the Y779F mutant of IRS4 (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by PUP-IT assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The preferential association of PIK3R2 appeared when comparing interaction proteins between WT and 5YF mutant of IRS4.
claims.source: Interestingly, this preferential association of PIK3R2 appeared again when comparing interaction proteins between WT and 5YF mutant of IRS4 (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by PUP-IT assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: The Y779F mutation of IRS4 exhibited dramatically decreased binding affinity with PIK3R2.
claims.source: Compared to the WT control, the Y779F mutation of IRS4 exhibited dramatically decreased binding affinity with PIK3R2, and subsequently decreased AKT phosphorylation as well (Figure 5H), indicating the importance of the tyrosine phosphorylation of the 779 residue (as mediated by FER) in recruiting PIK3R2 and AKT activation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: The Y779F mutation of IRS4 led to decreased AKT phosphorylation.
claims.source: Compared to the WT control, the Y779F mutation of IRS4 exhibited dramatically decreased binding affinity with PIK3R2, and subsequently decreased AKT phosphorylation as well (Figure 5H), indicating the importance of the tyrosine phosphorylation of the 779 residue (as mediated by FER) in recruiting PIK3R2 and AKT activation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: Both PIK3R1 and PIK3R2 can form complex with IRS4.
claims.source: Further co-immunoprecipitation assay demonstrated that both PIK3R1 and PIK3R2 can form complex with IRS4, and the presence of PIK3R1 wouldn't block the formation of the IRS4-PIK3R2 complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The presence of PIK3R1 wouldn't block the formation of the IRS4-PIK3R2 complex.
claims.source: Further co-immunoprecipitation assay demonstrated that both PIK3R1 and PIK3R2 can form complex with IRS4, and the presence of PIK3R1 wouldn't block the formation of the IRS4-PIK3R2 complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: PIK3R1 could form complex with both WT and Y779F mutant of IRS4 with equivalent binding affinity.
claims.source: More interestingly, unlike PIK3R2, PIK3R1 could form complex with both WT and Y779F mutant of IRS4 with equivalent binding affinity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Distinctive binding mechanisms were harnessed by PIK3R1 and PIK3R2, respectively, to form complex with IRS4.
claims.source: Therefore, distinctive binding mechanisms were harnessed by PIK3R1 and PIK3R2, respectively, to form complex with IRS4.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential binding patterns of PIK3R1 and PIK3R2 with IRS4 mutants.

claims.claim: OVCAR-5 cell lysates with anti-FER or anti-IRS4 antibody showed robust interaction between FER and IRS4 at endogenous level.
claims.source: Compared to anti-IgG control, the OVCAR-5 cell lysates with anti-FER or anti-IRS4 antibody showed the robust interaction between FER and IRS4 at endogenous level (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The interaction between FER and IRS4 disappeared upon CRISPR-Cas9-mediated KO of either FER or IRS4.
claims.source: Such interaction was disappeared upon CRISPR-Cas9-mediated KO of either FER or IRS4 (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Decreased tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4 was observed after FER KO in OVCAR-5 cells.
claims.source: We observed decreased tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4 after tandem IRS4 immunoprecipitation and pTyr immunoblotting (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The association of IRS4 and PIK3R2 was decreased in FER-deficient OVCAR-5 ovarian cancer cells.
claims.source: The association of IRS4 and PIK3R2 was also decreased in FER-deficient OVCAR-5 ovarian cancer cells (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: IGF1R phosphorylated IRS4 in the presence of ligand IGF1.
claims.source: IGF1R indeed phosphorylated IRS4 in the presence of ligand IGF1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: Small molecular IGF1R inhibitor BMS-536924 didn't decrease tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4 in the absence of IGF1.
claims.source: However, small molecular IGF1R inhibitor BMS-536924 didn't decrease tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4 in the absence of IGF1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B), indicating FER-mediated phosphorylation and activation of IRS4 in an IGF1-independent manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: FER-mediated phosphorylation and activation of IRS4 occurs in an IGF1-independent manner.
claims.source: However, small molecular IGF1R inhibitor BMS-536924 didn't decrease tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4 in the absence of IGF1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B), indicating FER-mediated phosphorylation and activation of IRS4 in an IGF1-independent manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that IGF1R inhibition doesn't affect IRS4 phosphorylation in the absence of IGF1.

claims.claim: IGF1R phosphorylated IRS4 probably in a Tyr779-independent manner.
claims.source: Moreover, IGF1R phosphorylated IRS4 probably in a Tyr779-independent manner, since mutating tyrosine 779 to phenylalanine didn't decrease phosphorylation level of IRS4 mediated by IGF1R receptor tyrosine kinase (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Y779F mutation doesn't affect IGF1R-mediated phosphorylation of IRS4.

claims.claim: TAE684 can robustly inhibit the auto-phosphorylation of FER at Tyr402, with IC50 around 8.8 nM.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, TAE684 can robustly inhibit the auto-phosphorylation of FER at Tyr402, with IC50 around 8.8 nM.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting and dose-response data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: No FES expression was detected in ovarian cancer cell lines used in this study.
claims.source: Interestingly, compared to lysates from myeloid leukemia cell HL-60, we detected no FES expression in ovarian cancer cell lines used in this study (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Ovarian cells treated with TAE684 showed dose-dependent inhibition on the kinase activity of FER.
claims.source: Of note, ovarian cells treated with TAE684 did show dose-dependent inhibition on the kinase activity of FER, as illustrated by pY402 FER blotting analysis (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Reduced global tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4 was observed in the presence of TAE684.
claims.source: Meanwhile, we witnessed the reduced global tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4, as well as decreased binding between IRS4 and PIK3R2 in the presence of TAE684 (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Decreased binding between IRS4 and PIK3R2 was observed in the presence of TAE684.
claims.source: Meanwhile, we witnessed the reduced global tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS4, as well as decreased binding between IRS4 and PIK3R2 in the presence of TAE684 (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The kinase activity of AKT was largely dampened upon TAE684 treatment.
claims.source: Of note, the kinase activity of AKT was largely dampened upon TAE684 treatment (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Re-expression of WT IRS4 in IRS4-KO cell line fully recovered the growth defect.
claims.source: Whereas re-expression of WT IRS4 in IRS4-KO cell line fully recovered the growth defect, 5YF mutants of IRS4 failed to rescue cell proliferation (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: 5YF mutants of IRS4 failed to rescue cell proliferation in IRS4-KO cells.
claims.source: Whereas re-expression of WT IRS4 in IRS4-KO cell line fully recovered the growth defect, 5YF mutants of IRS4 failed to rescue cell proliferation (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Cells re-expressing the Y779F mutant of IRS4 showed significantly delayed proliferation rate compared to the parental ovarian cancer cells.
claims.source: We did observe a certain extent of growth defect rescue with cells re-expressing in the Y779F mutant of IRS4, but these cells still showed significantly delayed proliferation rate compared to the parental ovarian cancer cells (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Re-expression of WT IRS4 in IRS4-KO cells exposed to U0126 treatment recovered the growth capacity to the same level as U0126 treatment alone.
claims.source: Consistently, IRS4 KO OVCAR-5 cells treated with U0126 demonstrated profound inhibition in cell growth (Figure 6F). Most importantly, re-expression of WT IRS4 in IRS4-KO cells exposed to U0126 treatment recovered the growth capacity to the same level as U0126 treatment alone, whereas 5YF mutant of IRS4 failed to rescue cell proliferation (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: 5YF mutant of IRS4 failed to rescue cell proliferation in IRS4-KO cells exposed to U0126 treatment.
claims.source: Most importantly, re-expression of WT IRS4 in IRS4-KO cells exposed to U0126 treatment recovered the growth capacity to the same level as U0126 treatment alone, whereas 5YF mutant of IRS4 failed to rescue cell proliferation (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: OVCAR-5 cells treated with TAE684 showed a dose-dependent growth inhibition.
claims.source: In addition, OVCAR-5 cells treated with TAE684 showed a dose-dependent growth inhibition, as illustrated by CTG assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-D.

claims.claim: Significantly delayed tumor formation was observed in mice injected with OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells with an empty vector compared to mice injected with OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells rescued with WT IRS4.
claims.source: Compared to mice injected with OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells rescued with WT IRS4, we observed significantly delayed tumor formation in mice injected with OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells with an empty vector (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Tumor growth in mice injected with OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells rescued with 5YF IRS4 was profoundly delayed compared to WT control.
claims.source: Consistent with our previous findings in cell cultures, the tumor growth in mice injected with OVCAR-5 IRS4-KO cells rescued with 5YF IRS4 was profoundly delayed compared to WT control (Figure 6G), further emphasizing the necessity of the tyrosine phosphorylation of key residues in IRS4 for ovarian tumorigenesis and progression.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of IRS4 in HEY and OVCAR-8 cells significantly accelerated tumor formations compared to parental controls.
claims.source: Consistently, ectopic expression of IRS4 in HEY and OVCAR-8 cells significantly accelerated tumor formations compared to parental controls (Figure 6H–K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 6H-K.

claims.claim: IRS4 shows the highest mRNA transcript abundance in the ovaries, followed by the thyroid gland and endometrium.
claims.source: Interestingly, IRS4 shows the highest mRNA transcript abundance in the ovaries, followed by the thyroid gland and endometrium (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data from the Human Protein Atlas dataset shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: A higher expression of IRS4 was observed in ovarian cancer patient samples compared to normal ovaries.
claims.source: In line with our findings in cell cultures, we observed a higher expression of IRS4 in ovarian cancer patient samples (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by tissue microarray data from the Human Protein Atlas database shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The expression levels of IRS4 in ovarian tumor samples were significantly elevated compared to normal control samples.
claims.source: In accordance with the result from HPA database, the expression levels of IRS4 in ovarian tumor samples were significantly elevated compared to normal control samples (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry staining data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: A lower expression of IRS4 was correlated to longer overall survival in patients with ovarian cancer.
claims.source: The result demonstrated that a lower expression of IRS4 was correlated to longer overall survival in patients with ovarian cancer (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by clinical data analysis from over 600 ovarian cancer patients shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: IRS4 was significantly overexpressed in ovarian cancers.
claims.source: In conclusion, IRS4 was significantly overexpressed in ovarian cancers and its upregulation was inversely correlated with survival and prognosis in ovarian cancer patients.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including immunoblotting, immunohistochemistry, and clinical data analysis.

claims.claim: Upregulation of IRS4 was inversely correlated with survival and prognosis in ovarian cancer patients.

results.result: Mass spectrometry analysis identified IRS4 as a novel FER substrate. Using two complementary approaches (in-gel and on-bead tryptic digestion), the authors identified 99 overlapping candidate FER substrates, including IRS4 and IGF1R.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C12 describe the mass spectrometry workflow and results with specific numbers of candidates identified. The dual approach with overlapping hits (C12) strengthens confidence. The identification of FER itself as a substrate (C13) serves as a positive control, validating the method. The data presentation in Figure 1 supports these claims.

results.result: FER binds directly to IRS4 through interaction between the FER kinase domain and both PH and PTB domains of IRS4. The binding is independent of FER kinase activity, while GRB2 recruitment to IRS4 is FER kinase activity-dependent.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C28 provide comprehensive domain mapping data using multiple truncation mutants and complementary approaches (co-IP, in vitro binding). The data consistently show that both PH and PTB domains of IRS4 interact with the FER kinase domain (not SH2 domain). The independence from kinase activity (C16) is well-demonstrated. However, attempts to identify specific charged residues mediating the interaction were unsuccessful (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), leaving the precise molecular mechanism unclear.

results.result: FER directly phosphorylates IRS4 on five major tyrosine residues (Y656, Y779, Y828, Y847, and Y921). Among seven non-receptor tyrosine kinases tested, FER showed the highest capability for IRS4 phosphorylation, and phosphorylation occurs in a dose-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C37 combine multiple lines of evidence: kinase specificity screening (C29), in vitro kinase assays (C30-C31), domain mapping (C32), mass spectrometry (C33-C34), and site-directed mutagenesis (C35-C36). The convergence of mass spec and mutagenesis data identifying five major sites is particularly strong. The 5YF mutant showing profoundly diminished phosphorylation (C36) validates these sites as the major FER phosphorylation targets.

results.result: IRS4 is upregulated in certain ovarian cancer cell lines (OVCAR-5 and OVCAR-3) and promotes cell proliferation through activation of the PI3K-AKT pathway. Loss of IRS4 decreases S-phase cells and proliferation without significantly affecting cell survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C46 demonstrate IRS4's role in ovarian cancer proliferation through gain-of-function (C39, C45) and loss-of-function (C40-C44, C46) experiments. The cell cycle analysis (C41) provides mechanistic insight. The rescue experiments (C43) strengthen causality. The correlation with AKT phosphorylation (C45-C46) links IRS4 to PI3K-AKT signaling. Multiple cell lines and complementary approaches support these conclusions.

results.result: PI3K-AKT pathway inhibition reduces OVCAR-5 cell proliferation in a dose-dependent manner, and compound library screening identified PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway inhibitors as the most effective class. Upon IRS4 deletion, ERK pathway activation increases as a compensatory mechanism, and dual inhibition of both pathways nearly completely blocks cell growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 demonstrate the importance of PI3K-AKT signaling and identify compensatory ERK activation. The compound library screen (C48) provides unbiased validation that PI3K-AKT-mTOR is critical for OVCAR-5 proliferation. The compensatory ERK activation (C49) and synergistic effect of dual inhibition (C50) reveal pathway crosstalk. However, the mechanistic basis for ERK upregulation upon IRS4 loss is not explored.

results.result: FER-mediated phosphorylation of IRS4 at Tyr779 is critical for recruiting PIK3R2/p85β. The Y779F mutation dramatically decreases PIK3R2 binding and AKT phosphorylation, as demonstrated by PUP-IT proximity labeling assays and co-immunoprecipitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 and C91 provide strong evidence using the PUP-IT proximity labeling system, which is well-suited for detecting weak/transient interactions. The preferential binding of PIK3R2 to WT vs Y779F mutant appears in multiple comparisons (C51-C52). Co-IP validation (C53-C54) confirms the PUP-IT results. The functional consequence (decreased AKT phosphorylation) links the biochemical observation to signaling output. This is a key mechanistic finding.

results.result: Both PIK3R1 and PIK3R2 can form complexes with IRS4, but they use distinctive binding mechanisms. PIK3R2 binding is phosphorylation-dependent (requires Y779), while PIK3R1 binds both WT and Y779F mutant with equivalent affinity.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 reveal an important distinction between PIK3R1 and PIK3R2 binding modes. The differential dependence on Y779 phosphorylation (C57) is well-demonstrated. This finding has biological significance given the different roles of PIK3R1 (tumor suppressive) and PIK3R2 (oncogenic) mentioned in the discussion. The data are clear and internally consistent.

results.result: Endogenous FER and IRS4 interact in OVCAR-5 cells, and genetic ablation of FER decreases IRS4 tyrosine phosphorylation and PIK3R2 recruitment. Ectopic FER overexpression increases, while FER knockout or pharmacological inhibition decreases, IRS4 phosphorylation and PIK3R2 recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 validate the FER-IRS4 interaction and functional relationship at endogenous levels. The reciprocal co-IP (C59) and specificity controls with KO cells (C60) are rigorous. The functional consequences on phosphorylation and PIK3R2 recruitment (C61-C62) connect the interaction to signaling. Claims C92-C93 extend this with gain- and loss-of-function approaches, providing comprehensive evidence for the FER-IRS4-PIK3R2 axis.

results.result: IGF1R phosphorylates IRS4 in the presence of IGF1 ligand, but FER-mediated phosphorylation of IRS4 occurs in an IGF1-independent manner. IGF1R likely phosphorylates IRS4 at sites other than Tyr779.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 distinguish FER-mediated from IGF1R-mediated IRS4 phosphorylation. The IGF1R inhibitor experiments (C64) demonstrate that FER acts independently of IGF1 signaling. The Y779F mutation not affecting IGF1R-mediated phosphorylation (C66) suggests different site specificity. This clarifies that FER provides an alternative, growth factor-independent mechanism for IRS4 activation, which is biologically important for the cancer context.

results.result: TAE684 inhibits FER kinase activity with IC50 ~8.8 nM and dose-dependently reduces IRS4 phosphorylation, PIK3R2 binding, AKT activity, and OVCAR-5 cell growth. FES is not expressed in the ovarian cancer cell lines tested, indicating TAE684's effects are FER-specific in this context.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C72 and C78 validate the FER-IRS4-PIK3R2-AKT axis using pharmacological inhibition. The IC50 determination (C67) establishes potency. The absence of FES expression (C68) addresses specificity concerns since TAE684 was originally identified as a FES inhibitor. The dose-dependent effects on the entire signaling cascade (C69-C72) and cell growth (C78) provide strong pharmacological validation of the genetic studies.

results.result: Re-expression of WT IRS4 rescues proliferation defects in IRS4-KO cells, but the 5YF phosphorylation-defective mutant fails to rescue. The Y779F single mutant shows partial rescue. These effects persist even when ERK pathway is inhibited with U0126.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C77 provide critical functional validation that IRS4 phosphorylation is required for its pro-proliferative function. The rescue experiments are well-controlled with empty vector controls. The partial rescue by Y779F (C75) vs complete failure of 5YF (C74) suggests Y779 is the most important but not the only functionally relevant site. The U0126 experiments (C76-C77) demonstrate that phosphorylation-dependent IRS4 function is required even when compensatory ERK signaling is blocked.

results.result: In xenograft models, IRS4 knockout significantly delays tumor formation, and this defect is rescued by WT IRS4 but not by the 5YF phosphorylation-defective mutant. Ectopic IRS4 expression accelerates tumor formation in IRS4-negative cell lines (HEY and OVCAR-8).
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 extend the in vitro findings to in vivo tumor growth. The rescue experiment design (C79-C80) is rigorous, showing that phosphorylation is required for IRS4's tumorigenic function. The gain-of-function experiments in IRS4-negative cells (C81) demonstrate sufficiency. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=4-7 per group). These data provide strong evidence that the FER-IRS4 phosphorylation axis is functionally important for tumorigenesis, not just cell culture proliferation.

results.result: IRS4 shows highest mRNA expression in ovaries among human tissues and is significantly overexpressed in ovarian cancer patient samples compared to normal ovaries. Higher IRS4 expression correlates with shorter overall survival in ovarian cancer patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C87 establish clinical relevance. The tissue expression pattern (C82) from HPA database provides context for why IRS4 is particularly relevant in ovarian cancer. Multiple independent datasets support overexpression in tumors: HPA tissue microarrays (C83), authors' IHC analysis (C84), and survival analysis from >600 patients (C85). The inverse correlation with survival (C85, C87) suggests IRS4 could be a prognostic marker. However, this is correlative data and doesn't prove causation.

results.result: Unlike IRS1 and IRS2, IRS4 lacks an SHP2 binding motif, which allows it to maintain constitutive hyperactivation of the PI3K-AKT pathway and promote growth factor-independent proliferation and tumorigenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 are supported by multiple citations to prior work. This provides important biological context for why IRS4 is particularly oncogenic - it cannot recruit the negative regulator SHP2. However, these are literature-based claims rather than new findings from this study. The authors don't experimentally validate this in their system, though their data showing IGF1-independent IRS4 phosphorylation by FER (C65) is consistent with this model.

results.result: The study reveals a kinase-substrate relationship between FER and IRS4 where FER-mediated phosphorylation enables PIK3R2 recruitment and PI3K-AKT pathway activation, promoting ovarian cancer cell proliferation and tumorigenesis. In IRS4-negative cells, FER regulates motility through the MET-GAB1-SHP2-ERK pathway instead.
results.evaluation: These claims (C90, C94, C95, C109, C111, C114) represent the main conclusions synthesizing the study's findings. They are well-supported by the comprehensive data presented. The context-dependent function of FER (C94-C95) reconciles this study with prior work showing FER's role in metastasis. Claim C114 about therapeutic potential is speculative but reasonable given the data. The overall model is internally consistent and supported by multiple experimental approaches.

results.result: Background claims establishing the clinical significance of ovarian cancer, the role of FER kinase in cancer, known FER substrates, and prior findings about FER in ovarian cancer.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C8, C96, C98, C102-C108, C117-C118) are background information supported by appropriate citations. They establish context but are not new findings. The citations appear appropriate and the claims are consistent with established knowledge in the field. These provide necessary background for understanding the significance of the current work.

results.result: Additional mechanistic details about IRS4 structure and FER-IRS4 interaction, including that IRS1 doesn't interfere with FER-IRS4 binding, weak phosphorylation of N-terminal IRS4 regions, and identification of YXXM motifs as potential PI3K binding sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C97, C99-C101 provide supporting mechanistic details. C97 shows IRS1 doesn't compete with IRS4 for FER binding. C99 notes weak phosphorylation in the 1-550aa region, suggesting additional minor sites. C100-C101 identify YXXM motifs that could serve as PI3K binding sites, providing structural context for the phosphorylation-dependent recruitment mechanism. These are well-supported but secondary findings.
